intro: Skip the islands and go north instead. This is the slow, cultural side of Thailand — the old capitals of Ayutthaya and Sukhothai, the temple-filled streets of Chiang Mai, the mountain village of Pai and the quiet north around Chiang Rai. You can do almost all of it overland: trains, buses and minivans, with the country rolling by outside the window. Here it is day by day, with real travel times, rough costs and where to stay.
chips: 🚐 Pai & Chiang Rai · the far north
quickAnswerHtml: The best northern Thailand itinerary runs Bangkok → Ayutthaya → Sukhothai → Chiang Mai → Pai → Chiang Rai over 10–12 days, almost entirely overland by train, bus and minivan. Give Bangkok 2 days, the two old capitals a day each, Chiang Mai 4, then loop up to Pai and Chiang Rai. Go in the cool season (Nov–Feb) for clear mountain air.
quickAnswerH2: The north in one line, no islands

blocks.html: The short version: start in Bangkok for 2 days, then head north through the old capitals — Ayutthaya and Sukhothai — before settling into Chiang Mai for temples, mountains and cooking classes. From there loop up the winding road to Pai, then across to Chiang Rai for the far-north temples and hill country. You can ride the scenic overnight train from Bangkok toward the north, and the rest goes by bus and minivan. Prefer more or fewer days? See the alternative lengths below.

blocks.html: Almost everyone lands here, and two days is enough before you head north. Do the big temples in the cool of the morning, ride a boat down the river, and eat your way through Chinatown after dark. Base yourself near the BTS or MRT so the traffic doesn't eat your time.

items: Day 1: the big hitters — the Grand Palace, Wat Pho's reclining Buddha, and Wat Arun across the river. See the Grand Palace & temples guide
Day 2: a market morning (Chatuchak on weekends, or a floating market), then Chinatown for street food — or slip in the easy day trip to Ayutthaya and start moving north

Day 3: Ayutthaya, the first old capital

blocks.html: An hour and a half north of Bangkok by cheap train lies Thailand's former royal capital — brick temples, crumbling prangs and the famous Buddha head cradled in tree roots, all flat enough to cycle between. You can do it as a day trip and sleep back in Bangkok, or overnight and carry on north the next morning. See Bangkok to Ayutthaya and the Ayutthaya city guide.

blocks.title: Rent a bicycle at the station
blocks.html: Rent a bicycle at the station — Ayutthaya's ruins are spread across a flat island, and pedalling between them in the morning light beats a coach tour hands down. Bring water; there's little shade among the brick.

blocks.text: Days 4–5: Sukhothai, where it all began

blocks.html: Push further north to Sukhothai, Thailand's very first capital and, for many, the most beautiful set of ruins in the country. The historical park is green, calm and made for cycling, with serene seated Buddhas reflected in old ponds. It sees a fraction of Ayutthaya's crowds. Trying to choose between the two? Read Sukhothai vs Ayutthaya — but on this route you get both. More on the town in the Sukhothai city guide.

items: Day 4: arrive and settle in New Sukhothai; a first evening ride out to the park for sunset among the ruins
Day 5: a full morning cycling the historical park, then afternoon on the road toward Chiang Mai (or an easy detour to nearby Si Satchanalai)

blocks.title: Where to stay in Sukhothai
blocks.text: New Sukhothai has the restaurants and buses; Old Sukhothai puts you at the park gates. Our ranked, review-checked picks:

blocks.html: This is the heart of the trip. Chiang Mai is cooler, calmer and greener than Bangkok — a moated old town packed with temples, mountains on the doorstep and Thailand's best café culture. Four days lets you slow right down. If you'd rather not do the full overland haul from Sukhothai, a short flight from Bangkok is always an option; see how to get from Bangkok to Chiang Mai (flight vs the scenic sleeper train).

items: Day 6: wander the old-town temples on foot (Wat Chedi Luang, Wat Phra Singh), then sunset at Doi Suthep above the city. Tickets on the Chiang Mai attractions page
Day 7: a morning at an ethical elephant sanctuary (choose no-riding, observation-first camps), then a Thai cooking class in the afternoon
Day 8: get up into the mountains — Doi Inthanon, Thailand's highest peak, with waterfalls and the twin royal pagodas, or a hill-tribe village day
Day 9: slow morning in a Nimman café, the Sunday Walking Street or Saturday market, and one last temple before the road north

blocks.title: Where to stay in Chiang Mai
blocks.text: The old town puts you walking distance from the temples, markets and cafés; Nimman is the modern, café-heavy side.
Day 10: Pai, up the winding road

blocks.html: The minivan from Chiang Mai to Pai takes about three hours and climbs through 762 numbered curves — genuinely twisty, so sit up front and take a motion-sickness tablet if you're prone. What waits at the top is worth it: a laid-back mountain town in a green valley, with hot springs, a canyon, waterfalls and viewpoints made for slow sunrises. See Chiang Mai to Pai and the Pai city guide.

blocks.title: The road to Pai has 762 curves
blocks.html: The road to Pai has 762 curves — that's not marketing, it's counted, and there's even a T-shirt. Motion-sickness pills, a front seat and a light breakfast make the three hours easy. Renting a scooter in Pai itself is popular, but only if you're already confident on two wheels.

blocks.title: Where to stay in Pai
blocks.text: Stay in walking distance of the walking-street strip, or out in the valley for rice-field views and quiet nights.
Days 11–12: Chiang Rai, the far north

blocks.html: Close the loop in Chiang Rai, the quietest of the northern cities and home to Thailand's most striking modern temples: the mirror-white Wat Rong Khun (the White Temple) and the deep-blue Wat Rong Suea Ten. Beyond them are tea and coffee hills, hot springs and the Golden Triangle where Thailand, Laos and Myanmar meet. Wondering how it compares to Chiang Mai or Pai? See Chiang Mai vs Chiang Rai and Pai vs Chiang Rai, and the Chiang Rai city guide.

items: Day 11: the White Temple in the morning (go early, before the tour buses), the Blue Temple and the black house (Baan Dam) in the afternoon
Day 12: the tea hills of Doi Mae Salong or the Golden Triangle, then fly home from Chiang Rai or bus back to Chiang Mai for onward flights

blocks.title: Where to stay in Chiang Rai
blocks.text: The centre keeps you near the night bazaar and buses; the outskirts trade convenience for hills and quiet.

blocks.title: Know before you go (for this route)

items.title: Go in the cool season, Nov–Feb
items.text: The north is at its best in the cool, dry months — clear mountain air and comfortable temperatures. Avoid Mar–Apr, when farmers burn fields and haze can settle over Chiang Mai and Pai. See best time to visit below.

items.title: The overnight train is scenic, not fast
items.text: The Bangkok–Chiang Mai sleeper takes roughly 11–12 hours and saves a night's hotel. Book a lower berth in second-class air-con ahead of time; it's the classic slow way to arrive in the north.

items.title: Minivans link the north
items.text: Sukhothai, Pai and Chiang Rai are mostly reached by bus or shared minivan. They're cheap and frequent, but the Pai road's 762 curves are twisty — sit up front and bring motion-sickness tablets.

items.title: Pack a layer for the mountains
items.text: Cool-season mornings on Doi Suthep, Doi Inthanon or in Pai can be genuinely cold. A light jacket or fleece is worth the packing space up north.

faq.q: How many days do you need for northern Thailand?
faq.a: Ten to twelve days is ideal for the full Bangkok → Ayutthaya → Sukhothai → Chiang Mai → Pai → Chiang Rai loop without rushing. In a week you can still see the highlights by dropping Sukhothai and Pai and flying Bangkok–Chiang Mai to save time.

faq.q: Can you do northern Thailand overland, without flying?
faq.a: Yes. The whole route works by train, bus and minivan. The scenic overnight sleeper links Bangkok toward the north in about 11–12 hours, and frequent buses and minivans connect Sukhothai, Chiang Mai, Pai and Chiang Rai. A short domestic flight is only worth it if you're tight on days.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit northern Thailand?
faq.a: The cool, dry season from November to February is best — clear mountain air and pleasant temperatures for temples and viewpoints. Avoid March and April, when agricultural burning can cause haze across Chiang Mai, Pai and Chiang Rai.

faq.q: Is the road to Pai really that winding?
faq.a: Yes — the Chiang Mai to Pai road has 762 counted curves and takes about three hours by minivan. It's genuinely twisty, so a front seat and a motion-sickness tablet make a real difference. The mountain valley at the end is worth it.

faq.q: Should I take the overnight train from Bangkok to Chiang Mai?
faq.a: It's a lovely, slow way to travel and it saves a night's accommodation, but it takes roughly 11–12 hours versus about an hour by plane. Take the sleeper for the experience and the scenery; fly if your days are limited. On this culture-first route, the train fits the pace well.
